chunks: Abu al-Husayn Muhammad ibn Harun al-Zanjani informed me, saying: Ali ibn Abd al-Aziz narrated to us, from Abu Ubayd, who said:
In the narration of the Prophet (peace be upon him and his Family) concerning a people who will emerge from the Fire and grow like a seed vegetates in what is carried by overflowing water.

Al-Asma'i said: The hameel is what the flood carries from all things; every carried thing is a hameel, just as it is said to the killed person: 'qateel' (the killed). From this stems the saying of Umar regarding the hameel: 'Inheritance is not passed except with proof.' It was called hameel because it was carried from its country as a small child and was not born into Islam.

Al-Asma'i said: As for the seed (habbah), for every plant that has a seed, the name of the seed from it is habbah. Al-Farra' said: The habbah is the sown seed of legumes. Abu Ubayd said: There is another interpretation for hameel, which is better than this: It is said that it is called hameel because its lineage is unknown. This is when a man says: 'This is my brother' or 'my father' or 'my son', and he is not believed except with proof, because he intends thereby to repel the inheritance of his master who freed him. For this reason, the adopted/unknown lineage person is called 'hameel'.
He said: Al-Kumait rebukes Qudha'a for their relocation to Yemen: 'Upon what you have settled, not from poverty * Nor hardship, is the station of the hameel.'

key_terms.الدَّعِيِّ: The adopted or person of unknown parentage
key_terms.حَمِيل: Debris carried by flood; also a term for a person of unknown lineage or adopted person

ai.seo_question: What is the meaning of 'hameel' in the hadith about those emerging from Hellfire?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq records this linguistic analysis to clarify the metaphor of 'hameel' in the hadith regarding those emerging from Hellfire, distinguishing between the physical debris carried by floodwaters and the genealogical concept of a person of unknown lineage (dii al-kunyah). This dual interpretation underscores the uncertainty of their status and origin, paralleling the need for proof of relation to claim inheritance, which reflects the theological nuance of their eventual deliverance.
